verdict: OK to lend in Ahmedabad cotton spinning, but only to spinners with export order books and low leverage; avoid weaving and processing units running at 50% capacity.
title: Ahmedabad Cotton Spinning & Yarn: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
**A spinning mill buys cotton and cotton yarn, runs it through spindles, and sells yarn to weavers, processors and exporters; cash comes back only after the yarn is sold and the buyer pays.** The value sits in the spread between cotton cost and yarn realisation, and in how much working capital is tied up in cotton and yarn inventory plus receivables [9]. Capex is heavy and fixed, so leverage and term-debt tenure decide who survives a downturn [8][10]. **So when a proposal lands, check the cotton-to-yarn spread and the inventory-plus-receivable days first; if the spread is thin and inventory days are long, ask how the unit funds the cotton peak.**

## What has broken in Ahmedabad now
**Local reporting is blunt: Ahmedabad weaving and processing units are running at around 50% capacity, some closing one or two days a week, with processing charges raised only about 5% to 7% against sharply higher cotton, yarn, coal and chemical costs [2].** Traders are restricting purchases for fear of holding high-cost inventory, and cotton yarn is short because spinning units have higher export commitments [2]. Ahmedabad and surrounding areas have around 200 weaving units [2]. **So when a weaving or processing proposal lands, check capacity utilisation and weekly closure days; if the unit is at 50% or shutting days, ask for the order book and decline unless there is a strong export buyer.** Note these local reports are from June 2026, five months old.

## Where the growth is
**The data pack is positive on the macro: Gujarat GST collections are up 11.9% Apr-to-date against India's 6.1%, and IIP NIC 13 output is up 13.1% YoY [D].** Peer results confirm the split: Nitin Spinners posted record quarterly revenue of Rs. 875 crores, up 10.3% YoY, with EBITDA margin at 17.78% [4][6], while Sportking's revenue fell 7.6% YoY though exports rose about 18% and EBITDA margin held at 12.0% [5]. **So pursue integrated spinners with export order books and diversified customers [11]; avoid stand-alone weaving and processing units dependent on local grey-fabric demand.**

## How to grow safely
**Structure term debt to match the spindle's cash cycle, keep leverage low, and take monthly stock and receivable statements plus GST returns.** Rating methodology is clear that low leverage and longer term-debt tenure protect coverage in a downturn [8][10], and that customer concentration stretches working capital when a big buyer delays [11]. **So when a proposal lands, check top-buyer share; if one buyer is above a third of sales, ask for the receivable ageing and set a covenant on it.**

## Early-warning signs
**Watch capacity utilisation, weekly closure days, cotton inventory days and buyer concentration.** If utilisation drops below 50% or closure days rise, ask for the order book and reduce exposure [2]. If inventory days stretch while cotton prices rise, ask how the position is hedged.
watch: Below 50% -> ask for order book and stop fresh limits [2]
Rising with cotton prices -> ask for hedge and reduce drawing power [9]
Above one-third -> covenant on receivable ageing [11]
Mismatch -> freeze limit and inspect godown [D]
